title: Rivers and seas
hookLine: rivers and seas rule a hundred valleys because they lie lower (Tao Te Ching 66)

cards: A good guide on a mountain trail walks in front, and nobody feels dragged. A good host fills the whole evening, and nobody feels crowded. A good coach is clearly in charge, and the players still feel it's their game.
Chapter sixty-one, a few days back, used a low river to describe a great country.
Chapter sixty-six brings the water back to describe one person who leads, and says the secret of those guides and hosts is the secret of the sea.

teach.b: First, kings of the valleys. In James Legge's translation, rivers and seas receive the tribute of all the valley streams because of "their skill in being lower than they." They don't conquer the streams or call them.
They're simply lower, so everything comes to them. The chapter calls that being king.
Second, words below, steps behind. The sage who wants to be above the people puts his words below them; wanting to lead them, he puts himself behind them.
An odd recipe for leadership: speak as if from underneath, walk at the back.
Third, nobody feels the weight. When such a person is above, the people feel no burden; in front, they feel no harm. So the whole world is glad to push this person forward, and doesn't tire of it.
Leadership, here, isn't grabbed. Others keep handing it to you, because you're easy to carry.

The chapter ends on a line the Tao Te Ching also uses in chapter twenty-two, which came up back on day nine hundred twenty-five: because this person doesn't compete, nobody in the world can compete with them.

It looks like the manager who asks before she tells, the older sibling who lets the younger one go first, the expert who explains without making anyone feel slow. They lie lower, and everything finds its way to them.

how: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter sixty-six as a picture of servant leadership: the one who leads speaks humbly, stays behind, and does not compete for the front.

games.q: you want to lead a group. chapter sixty-six describes how the sage ends up in front. how?
o: put words below them and self behind.
wait until someone names you leader.
games.why: the sage who wants to be above the people puts his words below them, and to lead them, puts himself behind them.

practice: Bring to mind one place where you're ahead of someone, older, more senior, or simply knowing more, and a moment there that's coming soon.
Try the chapter's recipe on it: words below, a question instead of an announcement; steps behind, a place to let them go first. Find one small way to lie a little lower, and hold it gently.
